head: Named after the road to Stratford Langthorne Abbey.
text: The Cistercian abbey was founded in 1135 and was one of the richest in England until Henry VIII closed it. This is not the Abbey Road of the Beatles, which is in St John's Wood.

head: Named after the woods by Lesnes Abbey.
text: The abbey was founded in 1178 by Richard de Luci; tradition says he did it in penance for his part in the quarrel that led to the murder of Thomas Becket. It was closed in the 1520s, and its ruins stand in a park near the station.

head: 'Acton' means the farm by the oak trees.
text: It comes from Old English āc, oak, and tūn, farm. 'Central' was added in the 1920s to tell it apart from Acton's other stations.

head: 'Acton' means the farm by the oak trees.
text: It comes from Old English āc, oak, and tūn, farm. 'Main Line' tells it apart from the other Actons: it is on the Great Western main line from Paddington.

head: 'Acton' means the farm by the oak trees.
text: The name comes from two Old English words: āc, oak, and tūn, a farm or settlement. The station opened in 1879 as Mill Hill Park and was renamed Acton Town in 1910.

head: Named after Aldgate, one of the gates in London's Roman and medieval wall.
text: Nobody is sure what 'Ald' means. Suggestions include 'old gate', an 'ale gate' with a tavern, a Saxon called Ealh, or a gate open to all. The gate itself was pulled down in 1761.

head: Named after Aldgate, an old gate in the City wall, and placed just east of it.
text: 'East' tells it apart from Aldgate station a short walk away. The origin of 'Aldgate' is uncertain: an old gate, an ale gate with a tavern, or a Saxon called Ealh are among the ideas.

head: Named after All Saints Church, the parish church of Poplar.
text: The church was built in the 1820s, when Poplar became a parish of its own. Its tall spire stands just north of the station.

head: 'Alperton' means the farm of a man called Ealhbeorht.
text: The Saxon name is an early form of Albert, and nothing else is known about him. The station opened in 1903 as Perivale-Alperton and took its present name in 1910.

head: 'Amersham' means the home of a Saxon called Ealhmund.
text: It was recorded in Anglo-Saxon times as Agmodesham, with -ham meaning a homestead. The Metropolitan Railway reached the town in 1892.

head: 'Anerley' is said to come from a northern word for 'lonely'.
text: The landowner, William Sanderson, called his house Anerley because it stood alone. He gave land for the railway on condition that a station was built, and it opened in 1839.

head: Named after the Angel, a famous coaching inn.
text: The inn stood at the junction of the Great North Road and Pentonville Road, where coaches stopped before the last stretch into London. It survived into the 20th century, and the station opened nearby in 1901.

head: Named after the bridge that carries Hornsey Lane over the road to the north.
text: The first archway was built in 1813 and replaced around 1900 by the iron bridge seen today. The station was called Highgate when it opened in 1907 and only became Archway in 1947.

head: The name probably recalls the Arnold family, landowners in the 14th century.
text: Over the centuries 'Arnold's Grove' seems to have become Arno's Grove and then Arnos Grove, though the link is not certain. The round station building of 1932 is one of Charles Holden's best known designs.

head: Named after Arsenal Football Club, whose old Highbury ground was next door.
text: The club was founded at the Royal Arsenal in Woolwich and moved to Highbury in 1913. The station opened in 1906 as Gillespie Road and was renamed in 1932, after a campaign by the club's manager Herbert Chapman. The old name can still be seen in the tiles.

head: Named after William Baker, who laid out the street in the 18th century.
text: The station opened in 1863 on the world's first underground railway, the Metropolitan Railway. Baker Street is also the fictional home of Sherlock Holmes, at 221B.

head: 'Balham' probably means a homestead in a rounded enclosure.
text: The place is in the Domesday Book of 1086 as Belgeham. The first part may come from an Old English word for something round or smooth.

head: Named after the Bank of England, which stands above the station.
text: The Waterloo & City line arrived here first, in 1898, in a station simply called City. Today Bank is one of the largest stations on the network, with several lines meeting under the old heart of the City.

head: 'Barbican' means a watchtower or outer defence of a fortified town.
text: The name probably recalls a tower on or near London's Roman and medieval wall. The station opened in 1865 as Aldersgate Street, after another gate in the wall, and only became Barbican in 1968.

head: 'Barking' means the people of Berica, or the settlement by the birch trees.
text: It was recorded as Berecingas in the 8th century. Barking Abbey, founded in the 7th century, was one of the most important nunneries in England.

head: Named after a new town on the banks of the Thames at Barking.
text: It is being built on the site of old power stations. The station opened in 2022 at the end of a new branch line.

head: 'Barkingside' means the Barking side of Hainault Forest.
text: The area lay just inside the old manor and parish of Barking, whose boundary ran through the forest. A map of 1777 shows 'Barking Side' as a long strip of common land on the forest's western edge.

head: An invented name, chosen around 1900 for new houses.
text: It has no known historical source. It was probably meant to sound grand and to pair with Earl's Court, the next station along.

head: Named after the power station next door, now shops, homes and offices.
text: Battersea itself is one of London's oldest recorded names: in the 7th century it was Badrices īeg, Badric's island, dry ground in the marshes by the Thames. The station opened in 2021 at the end of the Northern line extension.

head: 'Bayswater' recalls Bayard's Watering, recorded in 1380.
text: The Bayard family owned land here, by the River Westbourne, which now flows in a pipe under the streets. The 'watering' was probably a place where horses or cattle drank.

head: Named after Simon Adams Beck, governor of the Gas Light and Coke Company.
text: Work on the company's gasworks began here in 1868; it became the largest gasworks in the world. After it closed, its ruins were used as a film set, for example for Full Metal Jacket.

head: Named after Beckton and its park, recalling Simon Adams Beck of the Gas Light and Coke Company.
text: Beckton grew around the company's huge gasworks, begun in 1868. Besides gas, it produced by-products such as tar, dyes and fertiliser.

head: 'Becontree' probably means the tree of a Saxon called Beohha.
text: It was the name of an old meeting place of the local hundred, a unit of the county. After the First World War it was given to a huge new council estate, one of the largest in the world at the time.

head: 'Belsize' comes from the French bel assis, beautifully situated.
text: The name is recorded from the 14th century for an estate on the slopes below Hampstead. The station opened in 1907.

head: 'Bermondsey' means the island of a man called Beornmund.
text: The 'island' was a patch of raised dry ground in the marshes south of the Thames. The place is recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086, and the station opened in 1999 on the Jubilee line extension.

head: 'Bethnal' probably means the corner of a man called Blitha.
text: Early spellings such as Blithehale point to Old English blithe, happy, or a personal name, and healh, a corner of land. 'Green' was the open village green, which survives as a park.

head: Named after the black-robed Dominican friars, who had a priory here.
text: The friars moved here in the 13th century and stayed until Henry VIII closed the monasteries. Their name lives on in the bridge, the station and the area.

head: Named after the road, whose name is probably a corruption of Black House Lane.
text: The 'black house' was a local mansion, so the black horse on the station's tiles is a later idea. The station opened with the Victoria line in 1968.

head: 'Blackwall' means the dark embankment along the Thames.
text: The river wall was made of dark earth. Ships sailed from Blackwall in 1606 to found Jamestown in Virginia, the first lasting English colony in America.

head: Named after Sir Thomas Bond, who developed the street in the 17th century.
text: Bond bought land here and laid out the street. Today there is no street simply called Bond Street: it is made up of Old Bond Street and New Bond Street.

head: Named after the Borough of Southwark, the town at the south end of London Bridge.
text: For centuries this was London's main suburb, so it was simply called 'the Borough'. The station opened in 1890 on the first deep-level tube line.

head: Named after Boston Manor House, a Jacobean mansion near the station.
text: The name has nothing to do with Boston in Lincolnshire or Massachusetts: it probably goes back to a medieval name for the farm of a man called Bord. The station was called Boston Road until 1911.

head: Named after the le Bounde family, who owned land here in the 13th century.
text: Their name survived in a local farm, and the station took it when the Piccadilly line arrived in 1932.

head: Named after St Mary's Church, Bow, which stands on an island in the middle of the road.
text: Bow itself is named after a bow-shaped bridge over the River Lea, built in the early 12th century.

head: Named after the bow-shaped bridge over the River Lea.
text: The arched bridge was built in the early 12th century, by tradition at the wish of Queen Matilda, and gave its name to the village of Bow.

head: Named after the River Brent and a crossroads nearby.
text: 'Brent' is a Celtic name, much older than English, and may mean 'the holy one' or 'the high one'. The station opened in 1923 as Brent and became Brent Cross in 1976.

head: 'Brentwood' means the burnt wood.
text: In 1176 it was written in Latin as bosco arso, 'burnt wood': a forest partly cleared by fire. The town grew up on the road from London to Colchester.

head: 'Brixton' means the stone of a man called Beorhtsige.
text: The stone was probably a meeting place for the local hundred, an old unit of the county. The Victoria line reached Brixton in 1971.

head: 'Brockley' means the clearing of a man called Broca, or one where badgers live.
text: Old English brocc means badger, and lēah a clearing in a wood. The area grew in Victorian times, with many large villas.

head: 'Bromley' means a clearing where broom grows.
text: 'By-Bow' was added in 1968 to stop people confusing it with Bromley in Kent. Bow itself is named after a bow-shaped bridge over the River Lea.

head: 'Brondesbury' means the manor of a man called Brand.
text: It was one of the manors of St Paul's Cathedral, whose income went to one of the cathedral's canons.

head: Named after Brondesbury, the manor of a man called Brand, and a park estate built there.
text: The houses were built in the late 19th century on land of the old manor, which belonged to St Paul's Cathedral.

head: Named after Bruce Castle, a Tudor manor house in Tottenham.
text: The house is said to recall the Scottish royal family of Bruce, who held land in Tottenham in the Middle Ages. It is now a museum.

head: 'Buckhurst' means a wooded hill covered in beech trees.
text: It was first recorded in the 12th century as La Bocherste. The hill lies on the edge of Epping Forest, which still has many beeches.

head: 'Burnham' means the homestead by a stream.
text: It comes from Old English burna, stream, and hām, homestead. Nearby are Burnham Beeches, ancient woods famous for their old beech trees.

head: The name suggests a burnt oak tree, but its story is unknown.
text: It first appears in 1754 as the name of a field beside Watling Street, the old Roman road. Whatever oak gave the name is long gone.

head: Named after Bush Hill, an old name for the high ground here.
text: The estate was laid out in the 1870s and 1880s, and the station opened to serve it.

head: 'Bushey' probably means the enclosure near box trees.
text: It comes from Old English box, box tree, and hæg, an enclosure. The station is actually in Oxhey, on the Watford side.
